verdict.rationale: The canon positively attests two patterns that its own vocabulary refuses to rank. For support, 1 Corinthians 9:14 uses the aorist (a completed past action) verb "he arranged" or "he ordained" (diatexen), saying the Lord arranged that gospel proclaimers live from the gospel, and 1 Timothy 5:17-18 grants "laboring" (kopiontes) elders "double honor" (diple time) and quotes the wage maxim "the worker is worthy of his wage" (axios ho ergates tou misthou) verbatim from Luke 10:7. For self-support, Acts 18:3, Acts 20:34-35, and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 narrate Paul working with his hands and eating no bread "free of charge" (dorean). The hinge is the recurring noun "right" or "authority" (exousia), asserted five times across 1 Corinthians 9 (verses 4-18) and then, at 2 Thessalonians 3:9, expressly named as a right Paul possessed but declined, offering himself as a "pattern" or "example" (typos) to "imitate" (mimeisthai). Because a right may be exercised or surrendered, the lexicon establishes both forms as legitimate and ranks neither as the sole mandate, so any exclusive reading is contested while the both-valid claim is supported.

scripture.force: Paul affirms the "right" or "authority" (exousia) over the Corinthians yet says he did not use this right but endures all things so as not to hinder the gospel. The same noun that grounds the support pattern is here owned and then declined, the first half of the right-exercised-or-surrendered structure.

The aorist (a completed past action) verb "he arranged" or "he ordained" (dietaxen), the Lord arranged or ordained, plus the infinitive of living, establishes that those who proclaim the gospel may rightfully live from the gospel. The verb places material support of gospel workers within a dominical (from the Lord) arrangement, so support is a legitimate and authorized form.

Paul makes his "reward" or "wage" (misthos) the offering of the gospel "free of charge" (adapanon) so as not to make full use of his "right" (exousia) in the gospel. The verse shows that declining support is a voluntary choice taken precisely against an acknowledged right, not a denial that the right exists.

Elders who rule well, especially those "laboring" or "toiling to weariness" (kopiontes) in word and teaching, are to be counted worthy of "double honor" (diples times). The participle "to labor to the point of weariness" (kopiao) denotes wearying labor, and the following verse's wage maxim shows "honor" (time) here carries a material sense, supporting compensated teaching ministry.

Two scriptural maxims ground supporting laborers. The threshing ox not to be muzzled (citing Deuteronomy 25:4, verb "to thresh" (aloao)) and "the worker is worthy of his wage" (axios ho ergates tou misthou). The three terms "worker" (ergates), "worthy" (axios), "wage" (misthos) match Luke 10:7 word for word, so the formula "the Scripture says" (he graphe legei) here cites a dominical (from the Lord) saying and roots the supported pattern in canonical warrant.

Jesus instructs the seventy to remain in one house eating what is provided, for "the laborer is worthy of his wage" (axios ho ergates tou misthou autou). This dominical (from the Lord) saying, repeated at Matthew 10:10 with "worker" (ergates) and "food" (trophe), is the source quoted by 1 Timothy 5:18, supplying the gospel-side warrant that the support of workers is the Lord's own arrangement.

Paul, being "of the same trade" (homotechnon), being "tentmakers" (skenopoioi), "was working" (ergazeto, imperfect of continued action, meaning ongoing or repeated past action) at the craft. The narrative records sustained self-support by manual labor as an actual apostolic practice, evidencing the bivocational (working a trade alongside ministry) pattern.

Paul appeals to direct knowledge that "these hands" (hai cheires hautai) supplied his needs and those with him. The self-reference to manual provision presents bivocational (working a trade alongside ministry) support as a deliberate and exemplary apostolic choice.

By "laboring" (kopiontas) one "must" (dei) "help" or "support" (antilambanesthai) the weak. The same "to labor to the point of weariness" (kopiao) applied to compensated elders in 1 Timothy 5:17 is here applied to Paul's self-supporting toil, and the dominical (from the Lord) saying on giving and receiving frames self-support as a positive model, not a deficiency.

Paul ate no one's bread "free of charge" (dorean) but in toil and labor "working" (ergazomenoi) night and day so as not to burden anyone. The vocabulary of free provision refused and labor undertaken documents a chosen self-supporting practice.

The decisive qualifier: this was done not because we have no "right" (exousia) but to give ourselves as a "pattern" or "example" (typos) to "imitate" (mimeisthai). The same noun "right" (exousia) that anchors the support claim in 1 Corinthians 9 is named here as a right Paul holds yet surrenders, so self-support is presented as exemplary choice rather than a rule binding others.

complicating_texts.resolution: The dominical (from the Lord) directive that gospel workers may live from the gospel could be read as mandating support, but the same author four verses later (1 Corinthians 9:18) makes declining support his reward, and at 2 Thessalonians 3:9 classes that support as a "right" (exousia) he may forgo, and in Acts 18:3 he forgoes it. A right exercised or surrendered is not an exclusive obligation, so this text supports the legitimacy of support without excluding self-support.

Paul's continued tentmaking could be read as making self-support the only valid model, but 1 Corinthians 9:14 and the wage maxim of 1 Timothy 5:18 (quoting Luke 10:7) affirm a parallel right to support. The imperfect (ongoing or repeated past action) verb "he was working" (ergazeto) records what Paul did in his context, not a universal prohibition on receiving support, so it complicates an exclusive-support reading without overturning the validity of support.

The rule that one unwilling to work should not eat could be read as condemning supported ministry as idleness, but its target is "the disorderly" or "those acting out of order" (ataktoi, from atakteo, to be disorderly or idle) in verse 11, not gospel laborers, and 1 Timothy 5:17-18 treats "to labor to the point of weariness" (kopiao) in word and teaching as genuine wage-worthy labor. The text rebukes refusal to work, not the legitimate support of those who do labor in the word.

variants.note: No variant units supplied in the bundle, and these passages fall outside ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope per not_in_ecm_scope (the ingested ECM window is 3 John 1:1 to 1:15 only). The marginal sigla (textual apparatus marks) on surface tokens in Acts 18:3 and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 reflect apparatus markers but do not bear on the lexical patterns of work, right, and wage that drive the verdict, so the verdict is variant robust.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that elevates 1 Corinthians 9:14 and the wage maxim of 1 Timothy 5:17-18 into a mandate for paid ministry captures the genuine dominical (from the Lord) directive "he arranged" or "he ordained" (dietaxen) and the verbatim Luke 10:7 maxim "the worker is worthy of his wage" (axios ho ergates tou misthou), which give support real canonical weight. But it must explain away Paul's commended self-support in Acts 18 and 20 and his own statement at 1 Corinthians 9:18 and 2 Thessalonians 3:9 that support is a "right" (exousia) he may freely decline.

A reading that elevates Acts 18:3 and 2 Thessalonians 3:7-9 into a norm against paid ministry captures a real and repeatedly stressed apostolic example of working night and day. But 2 Thessalonians 3:9 itself denies the example is a binding rule by affirming the underlying "right" (exousia) to support, and 1 Corinthians 9:14 with 1 Timothy 5:18 root the support of workers in a directive of the Lord.

Holding the texts together by "the analogy of Scripture" or "Scripture interpreting Scripture" (analogia scripturae) yields a single coherent picture: a "right" (exousia) to support that may be exercised (1 Corinthians 9:14, 1 Timothy 5:17-18, Luke 10:7) or freely surrendered (1 Corinthians 9:12, 18; Acts 18, 20; 2 Thessalonians 3:8-9). This matches the lexical data on both sides without forcing either pattern to silence the other, and accounts for why the same author voices both.

hermeneutics.notes: Both clusters are read at face value in their own contexts and then harmonized by Scripture interpreting Scripture, since one author (Paul) articulates both the right and the chosen exception, and the recurring noun "right" or "authority" (exousia) is the explicit lexical bridge between them.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the New Testament establish exactly one legitimate mode of supporting those who lead and teach in the assembly, or does it attest more than one mode as valid?
stem_audit.notes: The proposition embeds two loaded elements. First, the closing clause that a particular tradition has favoured bivocational (working a trade alongside ministry) or lay eldership is a historical-tradition claim that the lexical store cannot evaluate and that lies outside the cultural air gap, so it is excluded from the verdict and the verdict rests only on the canonical patterns. Second, the framing both are valid; neither is the only legitimate form pre-asserts the conclusion, so the stem was neutralized to a genuine question before deriving the verdict on the lexical evidence alone. The lexical evidence independently supports the both-valid reading, so the verdict is not merely inherited from the stem.

lay_summary: The words show two patterns sitting side by side, and neither cancels the other. On one side, supporting those who teach is treated as a settled arrangement. In 1 Corinthians 9:14 the verb "he arranged" or "he ordained" (dietaxen) says the Lord arranged that those who announce the good news may live from it. In 1 Timothy 5:17 elders who rule well, especially those who "labor to weariness" (kopiao) in word and teaching, deserve double honor, and the next verse backs this with two maxims, the ox not muzzled while it threshes and the "worker" (ergates) "worthy" (axios) of his "wage" (misthos). Those three words match Luke 10:7 exactly, which is Jesus speaking, so the support side rests on the Lord's own saying. On the other side, the same apostle works with his hands. Acts 18:3 calls Paul and his hosts tentmakers with an imperfect verb (an ongoing or repeated past action) "he was working" (ergazeto) for ongoing labor. Acts 20:34 has him pointing to these hands as his provision. In 2 Thessalonians 3:8 he ate no one's bread "free of charge" (dorean) but worked night and day so as not to burden anyone. The hinge is one repeated noun, "right" or "authority" (exousia). Paul asserts this right five times across 1 Corinthians 9, then says in verse 12 and verse 18 that he chose not to use it, and at 2 Thessalonians 3:9 he states plainly that he worked not because he lacked the right but to make himself a "pattern" or "example" (typos) to "imitate" (mimeomai). That is the whole puzzle in one word. A right can be exercised or set aside, and the text records Paul doing both and commending both. So the vocabulary affirms that support is genuine and authorized, and that freely earning one's own keep is genuine and praiseworthy. What the words never do is rank one above the other or forbid either. Readers diverge because the canon hands them two patterns it does not rank, so the verdict is disputed in the sense that more than one practice is plainly legitimate rather than one being the single required form.
